paragraphs.text: Isolated glycolic aciduria is a metabolic condition caused by deficiency of glycolate oxidase (HAO1). Affected individuals have markedly increased urinary glycolic acid excretion with normal oxalate excretion, and the condition was asymptomatic in the reported individuals (Frishberg et al., 2014; McGregor et al., 2020).

paragraphs.text: Frishberg et al. (2014) reported 2 brothers, born to consanguineous healthy parents of Arab descent, who were evaluated for psychomotor delay associated with a triple-A-like syndrome (anisocoria, alacrima, and achalasia). The proband showed markedly increased urinary glycolic acid excretion with normal excretion of oxalate, citrate, and glycerate. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys with normal echotexture. The genetic basis of the triple-A-like syndrome in this family was found to be unrelated to the metabolic abnormality, and Frishberg et al. (2014) concluded that the glycolic aciduria was asymptomatic.

paragraphs.text: McGregor et al. (2020) identified, through exome sequencing of 2 population-based cohorts with substantial autozygosity (Born in Bradford and Genes and Health), a healthy woman of British-Pakistani ethnicity with complete germline knockout of HAO1. At the time of assessment she was in her fifth decade and was the mother of 3 healthy children. Renal ultrasound was normal; she was overweight (BMI 30 to 35 kg/m2) but otherwise healthy apart from common non-serious short-term illnesses and pregnancy symptoms. Standard clinical blood biochemistries were repeatedly normal over the previous decade, and her serum anion gap and plasma and urinary oxalate were normal. Her plasma glycolate (171 nmol/mL; reference, 14 or less) and urinary glycolate were markedly elevated, at 12 times and 6 times the upper limit of normal in healthy reference individuals, respectively. McGregor et al. (2020) concluded that lifelong HAO1 knockout in this woman was safe and without clinical phenotype.

paragraphs.text: In the woman with HAO1 knockout, McGregor et al. (2020) found urinary glycolate/creatinine ratios of 199 mg/g in a single void and 309 mg/g in a 24-hour collection (reference, 50 or less), with normal urinary oxalate and plasma glycerate. Plasma metabolomics and lipidomics (1,871 biochemicals) showed that most metabolites were similar to those of 25 controls, but 18 biochemicals, including glycolate, were markedly elevated (more than 5 SD above controls). Elevated cholic acid-related compounds were thought possibly to reflect reduced availability of glycine for conjugation, with unconjugated bile acids elevated and glycine- and taurine-conjugated bile acids reduced. Six of the significantly elevated metabolites had structures compatible with being potential HAO1 substrates. By comparison with data from healthy volunteers treated with lumasiran, an RNA interference therapeutic targeting HAO1, in whom maximal plasma and urinary glycolate concentrations at the highest dose were 3 to 5 times less than in this woman, McGregor et al. (2020) estimated that she likely retained less than 2% residual glycolate oxidase activity.

paragraphs.text: In a healthy British-Pakistani woman with markedly elevated plasma and urinary glycolate, McGregor et al. (2020) identified a homozygous 1-bp deletion (c.997delC) in the HAO1 gene, predicted to cause a frameshift (Leu333SerfsTer4) truncating the final 37 amino acids of the protein. The variant was found by exome sequencing and confirmed in blood DNA sequencing reads and by Sanger sequencing of a separate saliva DNA sample. She was not homozygous for any other rare predicted loss-of-function genotypes. Since HAO1 is normally targeted to hepatocyte peroxisomes by a C-terminal SKI tripeptide, which the mutant protein is predicted to lack, the authors expressed the mutant in CHO-K1 cells; the Leu333SerfsTer4 protein showed markedly reduced levels, with unaffected mRNA levels, and was diffusely distributed (mislocalized) within cells.

(2020) noted that HAO1 silencing is the mechanism of lumasiran, an investigational RNA interference therapeutic for primary hyperoxaluria type 1, and concluded that the absence of a clinical phenotype in a woman with lifelong HAO1 knockout supported the potential safety of chronic HAO1 inhibition. agent.process_note: I read both papers in full: the abstract of Frishberg et al. (2014), which is the only part available, and the full text of McGregor et al. (2020). HAO1 was established as the causal gene from these papers, with homozygous mutations in both reports. No HGNC reference data were supplied, so I left out the HAO1 MIM number and cytogenetic band. The chromosome 20 location comes from the GRCh37 coordinate given by McGregor et al. (2020). The Frishberg abstract does not say whether the second brother was tested for glycolate or genotyped, so I attributed the biochemical findings only to the proband. McGregor et al. cite earlier reports (Clifford-Mobley 2017, Craigen 1996) that are not in the folder, so I left them out.
